## The idea

An arrangement can be harmonically correct and still sound muddy. Two voices
that occupy the same register, use similar envelopes, and sit in the same
stereo position compete for the same perceptual space. Turning one down changes
the balance, but it often leaves the overlap intact.

*Register* is pitch height, *timbre* is the spectral character of a sound, and
space includes stereo position and apparent depth. Separate voices along one or
more of these dimensions. Move one part an octave, choose a shorter envelope,
pan it away from its neighbour, or place it farther back with reverb.

I treat volume as the final balance control. First give each musical role a
place where it can be identified.

## Run this

One harmonic skeleton is rendered three ways. The sparse version leaves roles
out. The dense version crowds them into the middle register. The wide version
spreads register, timbre, pan, and depth.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78

progression = [
  chord(:c3, :minor),
  chord(:ab2, :major),
  chord(:eb3, :major),
  chord(:bb2, :major)
]

define :render_skeleton do |chords, layout|
  chords.each do |notes|
    if layout == :sparse
      use_synth :piano
      play notes.first, release: 1.8, amp: 0.7
      play notes.last + 12, release: 1.2, amp: 0.6
    elsif layout == :dense
      use_synth :saw
      play_chord notes.map { |pitch| pitch + 12 }, release: 1.8, amp: 0.55
      play_chord notes.map { |pitch| pitch + 15 }, release: 1.8, amp: 0.5
    else
      with_fx :reverb, room: 0.7, mix: 0.35 do
        use_synth :hollow
        play notes.first, release: 2.4, amp: 0.55, pan: -0.5
      end
      use_synth :pluck
      play notes.last + 24, release: 0.7, amp: 0.65, pan: 0.55
    end
    sleep 2
  end
end

render_skeleton progression, :sparse
sleep 1
render_skeleton progression, :dense
sleep 1
render_skeleton progression, :wide
```

The dense pass piles related saw spectra into one band. The wide pass gives the
low sustained tone and high pluck separate locations and envelopes.

## Change one thing

1. In the wide layout, remove + 24 from the pluck. Its attacks now overlap the
   low part's register. Listen for pitch identity becoming harder to follow even
   though the pan positions remain.
2. Set both pans to 0. The parts return to the centre, but register and envelope
   still separate them. This reveals how much work each dimension contributes.
3. Raise the reverb mix to 0.75. The sustained voice moves farther back and
   loses definition. Restore the value, then add a short echo to the pluck and
   compare depth without changing notes.

## Why it works

Masking occurs when sounds compete in similar frequency bands at similar
times. Register separation reduces spectral overlap. Contrasting envelopes
separate attack and sustain. Panning gives the ears different level and timing
cues, while reverb changes the ratio of direct to reflected sound.

These controls interact. A low saw has many upper partials, so moving its
fundamental down does not guarantee a clear middle register. A sine-like bass
leaves more room. A long reverb can refill the gaps created by a short release.
Change one dimension, listen, then inspect the next collision.

The harmonic skeleton remains data. Layout is a rendering argument. This makes
orchestration comparable: the same progression passes through sparse, dense,
and wide configurations without duplicated chord arrays. It also keeps a muddy
rendering from being mistaken for a harmony error.

Effects create depth only in relation to a drier foreground. If every voice
uses the same large room and mix, the entire image recedes. Assign space by
role, and audition on headphones and speakers because low-frequency response
changes the result.

## Take it further

Arrange one eight-bar harmonic skeleton in three versions: sparse, dense, and
wide. Keep chord data identical. The sparse version may use two roles, the
dense version at least four, and the wide version must separate every role by
two of these dimensions: register, synth, envelope, pan, or effect depth.
Write a one-line diagnosis for each collision you hear and fix it without
changing chord roots or lowering the master amplitude.
